blocks.text: Keep the color labels in order, then correct and extend them.
[item1, item2, ...] creates a list: an ordered collection that can change.
items[0] selects the first item. Negative indices count from the end.
items[start:stop] returns a new list from start up to, but excluding, stop.
items[index] = value replaces the item at that position.
items.append(value) adds a value at the list’s end.
Track label positions through the replacement and append. Replacement changes an existing position; append extends the end. The slice selects a range into a new list, excluding its stop position.
A slice’s stop is excluded. A slice returns a new list, unlike a single-index lookup; replacing an item is different from appending.

blocks.code:
labels = ["red", "blue", "green"]
print(labels[0])
print(labels[-1])
labels[1] = "navy"
labels.append("yellow")
print(labels[1:3])
print(labels)

annotations.text: Replace the existing label at this position.

blocks.text: Collect distinct color labels rather than repeated occurrences.
A set is unordered and contains distinct elements. set(items) constructs it, removing repeated values.
{item1, item2, ...} makes a nonempty set. set() makes an empty set; {} makes a dictionary.
value in values tests membership in a set.
a | b is union: elements in either set. a & b is intersection: elements in both.
Compare the label sets by membership, not display order. Repeated source labels contribute one distinct element. Union combines membership from either set; intersection keeps only shared members.
set() is an empty set, whereas {} is a dictionary. Sets do not provide stable first and second sequence positions.

blocks.code:
first = set(["red", "blue", "red"])
print(first)
second = {"blue", "green"}
print("red" in first)
print(first | second)
print(first & second)
empty = set()

annotations.text: Repeated source labels contribute one distinct element.
The resulting set contains red and blue once each. Their displayed order is not a stable sequence order.
Union includes members from either set.
Intersection includes members shared by both sets.

public.prompt: Convert the list assigned to first into a set to remove repeated labels, then test whether "red" belongs to first. Assign membership using label to member. Also assign the union of first and second to combined and their intersection to shared. Write the set conversion and each expression yourself.

solution_files.content:
first = ["red", "blue", "red"]
label = "red"
second = {"blue", "green"}
first = set(first)
member = label in first
combined = first | second
shared = first & second

spec.expr:
(lambda scope: (exec('import ast
tree = ast.parse(open("main.py").read())
_skill_ok = all(any(isinstance(n, k) for n in ast.walk(tree)) for k in (ast.In, ast.BitOr, ast.BitAnd)) and any(isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Name) and n.func.id == "set" for n in ast.walk(tree))
', scope), ([sorted(first), member, sorted(combined), sorted(shared)]) if scope["_skill_ok"] else None)[1])(globals().copy())
